title: Pajero / Montero (Third Generation)
verdict: Mitsubishi bet the company argument on a monocoque with a frame welded underneath, gave it four-wheel independent suspension, and then won the Dakar with its descendants five years running. Diehards still call it soft. Keep the timing belt and the brake booster healthy and it's one of the best-riding cheap overlanders you can buy.
codes: V63W · V65W · V68W · V73W · V75W · V78W

paragraphs: The first two Pajeros had sold 1.26 million worldwide, according to Mitsubishi, and the [[pajero/pajero-gen2|second generation]] was still a hit when the third was planned. The threat was the crossover SUV: buyers wanted car-like manners on the road. Mitsubishi says the decision on how to answer it split the company. In the end it dropped the separate ladder frame and built a monocoque body with a frame structure welded into its floor. The new Pajero went on sale in Japan in the autumn of 1999 and reached most export markets as a 2001 model.

story.heading: THE ARGUMENT THAT SPLIT MITSUBISHI
paragraphs: Mitsubishi's own history admits the trade-off. A monocoque is lighter, but a frame is better at the rigidity and durability that rough tracks demand. Its answer was the 'built-in frame' monocoque, and the company says that although the truck grew, it lost a lot of weight and met an internal target of body stiffness comparable to its Dakar prototypes. Wikipedia credits Mitsubishi's RISE safety structure for a cabin that held its shape well, and the fuel tank moved between the axles to help weight distribution and ground clearance.

The suspension changed just as much. Double wishbones and coil springs went in at the front, replacing torsion bars, and the rear became independent too, on a subframe. The idea came from the rally team: the [[pajero/pajero-gen2|Pajero Evolution]] had used independent rear suspension, and Wikipedia says that design set the pattern for the third generation. Rack-and-pinion steering replaced the old recirculating-ball box. Unsealed 4X4 called the Australian NM 'the first 4×4 wagon in its class with monocoque construction and a fully independent suspension system'.

story.heading: SUPER SELECT II, GDI AND A NEW DIESEL
paragraphs: Super Select became Super Select 4WD II. The centre differential uses planetary gears and splits torque between 33:67 and 50:50 front to rear, and the modes are now switched electrically. You still get 2H, full-time 4H, and locked-centre high and low ranges. Engines were a mix of old and new: the 6G74 3.5 V6 carried over (as a GDI direct-injection engine in Japan), the 2.8 4M40 diesel stayed in some markets, and a new 3.2-litre 4M41 DI-D four arrived. Mitsubishi Japan lists the 3.2 DI and 3.5 GDI as the two engines developed for the new truck.

Australia got the NM in 2000 with a launch drive to the Lambert Centre that a freak downpour turned into a mud epic. Unsealed 4X4's Dean Mellor remembers the petrol V6s refuelling from jerry cans while the 2.8 diesels 'made it on the smell of an oily rag'. In 2002 the 3.2 DI-D replaced the 2.8 there, and it could be ordered with the five-speed automatic. A 3.8 V6 followed in 2003, and electronic traction control arrived in 2004, ahead of the Prado.

story.heading: AMERICA: THE MONTERO LIMITED AND THE MOOSE TEST
paragraphs: The US got the long-wheelbase five-door only, as the Montero XLS and Limited, with the 3.5 V6 rated at 200 hp and 235 lb-ft. Its first year brought bad press. In May 2001 Consumer Reports put the Montero Limited through its short-course avoidance manoeuvre, and its test truck tipped up on two wheels in eight of nine runs at 36.7 mph or faster. CR rated it 'Not Acceptable', a verdict it had previously given only the Suzuki Samurai and the 1996 [[trooper/trooper-2|Isuzu Trooper]] and Acura SLX. Mitsubishi disputed the method, said it had no stability complaints from customers and quoted NHTSA's view that CR's test had no scientific basis.

For 2003 the Montero was facelifted and the 3.5 gave way to a 3.8-litre 6G75 rated by Bring a Trailer's listings at 215 hp and 248 lb-ft, with Mitsubishi's M-ASTC stability and traction control. Owners on Expedition Portal say the XLS was dropped after 2003, leaving only the Limited. The Montero was Mitsubishi's only American SUV with standard four-wheel drive rather than all-wheel drive, and it left the US market after the 2006 model year.

story.heading: LEGACY
paragraphs: The third generation was replaced in Japan in October 2006, but the platform didn't die. The fourth-generation Pajero kept the monocoque-and-frame body and independent suspension, and Unsealed notes that the same basic structure was still on sale in Australia two decades after the NM. In China, GAC Changfeng built the third generation until 2011. Today it's a bargain: Bring a Trailer has sold US Monteros for under $20,000, and the Japanese 3.2 diesels are now old enough to import. It rides like a car and has the [[land-cruiser/100-series|100 Series]]'s cabin space, according to Unsealed, though its IFS-and-IRS layout will always start an argument at the campsite.

callout.label: SIDEBAR · DAKAR 2000–2005
callout.title: Five wins in a row
paragraphs: Mitsubishi's works team switched to a T2 rally car based on the new Pajero for the 2000 Dakar. It kept the production monocoque, stretched the wheelbase, used four-wheel independent suspension and ran a 3.5 MIVEC V6. That year Jean-Louis Schlesser's buggy won, and Mitsubishi had to settle for third.

Then the streak began. In 2001 Jutta Kleinschmidt became the first woman to win the Dakar outright, in a Pajero, after Hiroshi Masuoka broke a half shaft fighting the Schlesser buggies. Masuoka won in 2002 and again in 2003, the second year in a tube-framed Pajero Evolution prototype whose body only looked like the road car. Unsealed 4X4 counts five consecutive wins from 2001 to 2005, and Mitsubishi says its last Dakar win came in 2007.

engineering_intro: The big change is structural: a monocoque with a ladder-type frame welded into the floor, not a body bolted to a separate chassis. The suspension is independent at all four corners on coil springs, steering is rack and pinion, and Super Select 4WD II gives full-time 4WD with a lockable planetary centre differential. US Monteros are long-wheelbase V6 automatics; elsewhere you'll find three-door short bodies and the 3.2 DI-D diesel.

engineering.note: Mitsubishi Japan describes a frame structure welded to the underside of the monocoque body.
The US got only the long-wheelbase five-door.

engineering.v: Double wishbones front · independent rear on a subframe
engineering.note: Coil springs at all four corners. Mitsubishi's Japanese history calls the rear double wishbone; its English history says multi-link.
Electrically switched. Planetary centre diff, 33:67 to 50:50 torque split, locking centre in 4HLc and 4LLc.
BaT's 2001 Limited has a limited-slip rear. ARB sells a rear Air Locker for the 9.5 in IRS diff.
V6s use timing belts; the 4M41 has a chain.

buying_checks.head: Ask for the timing-belt receipt
buying_checks.body: Both US V6s use belts, and owners on Expedition Portal call them interference engines. One owner quotes the manual at 105,000 miles for 2001–2006 Monteros. If there's no proof, budget for a belt, tensioner, pulley, water pump and seals; owners quoted $700 at an independent shop to about $1,400 at a dealer.

buying_checks.head: Test the brakes cold, and listen for the booster
buying_checks.body: Third-gen trucks use a hydraulic brake booster (HBB) with an accumulator. Recalls covered the accumulator in the US (01V254001), Australia and Hong Kong. Listen for an ABS-pump noise or tone, and check for a hard pedal on the first stop after the truck has been parked. One 2002 owner paid about $2,000 to replace the whole HBB system.

buying_checks.head: Look under it for oil and ATF cooler leaks
buying_checks.body: Owners on Expedition Portal chase leaks from the engine-oil and transmission-cooler hoses where they run along the frame and join the oil pan and cooler. Bring a Trailer's 2001 Limited had its oil-cooler lines replaced before sale.

buying_checks.head: Cycle the Super Select lever
buying_checks.body: Go through 2H, 4H, 4HLc and 4LLc on loose ground. CarsGuide's expert says a flashing 4WD light on these trucks usually points to the front-diff actuation system: solenoids, vacuum lines, actuator or diff sensor. BaT's 2001 Limited needed new transfer-case switches.

buying_checks.head: Feel for driveline clunk
buying_checks.body: Australian NM owners report a clunk when going from off-throttle to on-throttle. One dealer replaced the diff centre and drive rods, which only helped a little. Owners say it didn't get worse with mileage, but factor it into the price.

buying_checks.head: Check rear ride height
buying_checks.body: Several NM/NP owners on ProductReview say the rear sags with age, and an ExplorOz owner scraped the side steps and towbar until he fitted a 40 mm ARB kit. Look for a nose-up stance and worn rear bushings.

buying_checks.head: Identify the engine, and don't expect a ladder frame
buying_checks.body: JDMBUYSELL warns buyers that there's no separate chassis, that the 4M41 uses a chain while the V6s use belts, and not to accept a common-rail claim on a 1999 diesel without proof. Check the chassis code on the plate.

buying_checks.head: Run the VIN for recalls
buying_checks.body: US recalls include the brake-booster accumulator (01V254001, 2001–02), a fuel-tank leveling valve that can leak (04V319000, 2002–04), and label campaigns. In Australia, REC-003136 covers 13,488 NM/NP trucks for the same accumulator.

repairs.title: Timing belt, tensioner and water pump (6G74 3.5 / 6G75 3.8)
repairs.cost: Owners quoted about $700 (independent) to $1,400 (dealer) for the full job
repairs.symptoms: Usually none before it fails. Owners on Expedition Portal call both US V6s interference engines and quote the manual's 105,000-mile interval for 2001–2006 Monteros. On a 2001 NM, an Australian owner's tensioner disintegrated at about 110,000 km.
repairs.fix: Following an Expedition Portal write-up: drain the coolant, remove the fan and shroud (the radiator can stay in if you protect it), then the accessory belts, accessories and main bracket. Hold the crank pulley and remove it, then the timing covers. Refit the crank bolt with spacers so you can turn the engine, and set TDC on the cam and crank marks. Remove the old tensioner and pulley, fit the new belt keeping the driver's side tight (large binder clips hold it on the cam gears), and fit the new tensioner without pulling its pin. Lever the pulley into the belt until the pin slides freely, torque the pulley bolt, rotate the crank two turns, wait five minutes and check the tensioner piston protrusion against the service manual. Replace the water pump, front seals and crank bolt while you're there, and the O-ring on the pipe behind the water pump, which owners say is often missed. One owner gives the crank-pulley bolt torque as 130 lb-ft; confirm it in the manual.
repairs.tools: Crank-pulley holding tool (owners make one from flat steel) · large binder clips · torque wrench · non-marring pry bar · service manual · coolant.

repairs.title: Diagnose the hydraulic brake booster (HBB) and accumulator
repairs.time: ≈ 1 hour to check the recall; half a day to replace parts
repairs.cost: Recall work is free; one owner paid about $2,000 for a complete HBB system
repairs.symptoms: A hard pedal or slow brake assist on the first stop after the truck has been parked, an ABS-pump noise, a warning lamp or buzzer, or a pump that runs constantly. The US, Australian and Hong Kong recalls say a faulty accumulator can leak its nitrogen charge. A 2002 Limited owner on Expedition Portal had intermittent ABS tones, then a total loss of boost and a seized pump motor that drained the battery.
repairs.fix: Run the VIN for NHTSA 01V254001 (US 2001–02) or Australia's REC-003136 and have any open accumulator recall done first. JDMBUYSELL relays Mitsubishi's warning that spilled brake fluid can get into the pump motor: wipe up spills and never wash fluid away with water. A warning lamp, buzzer or weak assist needs Mitsubishi's tester to diagnose. The Expedition Portal owner's dealer blamed debris in the fluid, and owners there recommend regular brake-fluid flushes as these trucks age.
repairs.tools: Scan tool or dealer tester · brake bleeder · DOT 3 fluid · battery charger.

repairs.title: Replace leaking oil and ATF cooler hoses
repairs.cost: OEM hoses, copper washers and fluid
repairs.symptoms: Oil or ATF drips under the engine, wet hoses along the frame, a low transmission level. Owners trace leaks to the joints at the oil pan and the oil cooler, and one found a line that had chafed on the frame.
repairs.fix: Remove the skid plate and the two brackets that hold the hoses to the frame. Soak the fittings in penetrating oil first; one owner twisted a hose at its fitting and had to cut it off with tin snips. Fit new OEM hoses with new copper washers (don't reuse them), and protect any line that touches the frame with a split piece of old hose and zip ties. Top up or refill with the right fluids: owners insist on Mitsubishi Diaqueen SP-III in the automatic.
repairs.tools: Line wrenches · penetrating oil · tin snips · new copper crush washers · drain pans · funnel.

repairs.title: Cure a flashing 4WD light (Super Select II)
repairs.cost: Usually a solenoid, hose, switch or sensor
repairs.symptoms: The 4WD indicator keeps flashing after you shift, or the front axle won't engage.
repairs.fix: CarsGuide's expert says it's 'likely to be a problem with the actuation system for the front diff' and lists the solenoids, vacuum line, actuator and diff sensor. Start with the cheap parts: check every vacuum hose to the front-diff actuator for cracks and loose ends, test the solenoids, then the actuator and sensor. Bring a Trailer's 2001 Limited had its transfer-case switches replaced, so check those and their wiring too. Afterwards, cycle through every mode on loose ground and use 4WD regularly.
repairs.tools: Hand vacuum pump with gauge · multimeter · scan tool · basic hand tools.

repairs.title: Chase the on/off-throttle driveline clunk
repairs.cost: From a grease gun to diff mounts and bushings
repairs.symptoms: A heavy clunk from the driveline when you go from off-throttle to on-throttle. NM owners on ExplorOz report it from about 50,000–60,000 km, and say Mitsubishi called it a known issue with no fix at the time.
repairs.fix: Rule out the simple causes first. Grease the tailshaft slip joint (one ExplorOz contributor found a dry slip joint caused the same clunk on another 4x4), then check the rear diff mounts, the rear subframe and control-arm bushings, and the CV joints for play. One owner's dealer replaced the diff centre and drive rods and got only a small improvement. Owners note that shifting to 4H removes the backlash, and that the clunk didn't get worse over 110,000–120,000 km.
repairs.tools: Jack and stands · pry bar · grease gun · flashlight.

repairs.title: Refresh tired rear springs, shocks and bushings
repairs.cost: Springs, shocks and bushings, plus an alignment
repairs.symptoms: A sagging rear, scraping side steps or towbar, and a floaty or clunky rear end. Several NM/NP owners say the rear sags with age, and one ExplorOz owner fixed scraping with a 40 mm ARB lift.
repairs.fix: Support the body and rear subframe, remove the rear shocks, and drop the control arms enough to release the coil springs. Fit new coils matched to your load (Old Man Emu offers medium- and heavy-duty rear coils for the NM) and new shocks. Replace worn control-arm bushings while it's apart. Torque the suspension bolts at ride height, not hanging, then get a four-wheel alignment.
repairs.tools: Jack and stands · spring compressor if needed · torque wrench · bushing press or puller · alignment afterwards.

repairs.title: Replace the starter motor
repairs.cost: A starter and an hour or two
repairs.symptoms: Clicking or slow cranking with a good battery. Starters are the most common complaint in ProductReview's NM/NP owner reviews; one owner says they 'started to go like hot cakes'.
repairs.fix: Charge and load-test the battery and clean the terminals and earth strap first. Then disconnect the battery, remove the skid plate if fitted, unplug the solenoid lead and main cable, and unbolt the starter. Fit the new unit, torque the bolts, reconnect and test. On a 4M41 diesel, check the glow plugs and battery health too, since a weak battery cranks a diesel slowly.
repairs.tools: Battery load tester · socket set with extensions · multimeter.

faq.q: What's the biggest tire I can fit without a lift?
faq.a: About 33 inches if it's narrow. Owners on Expedition Portal run 235/85R16 and 255/85R16 (about 33 in) on stock suspension with no rubbing, and one '05 owner runs LT265/70R17. A 285/75R16 is a step too far: owners report it rubbing at full lock even with an OME lift. A veteran owner's advice is that '265/75R16 or 17 are the best fit on these rigs, even lifted.' Stock tires on BaT's 2001 Limited are 265/70R16.

No. It's a monocoque with a frame structure welded into its floor, which Mitsubishi calls a built-in frame. Mitsubishi says the design was lighter than the old ladder frame and as stiff as its Dakar prototypes, but JDMBUYSELL warns that it's not for buyers who want a separate chassis.

faq.q: Can I drive in 4WD on the highway?
faq.a: Yes, in 4H. Super Select 4WD II's centre differential splits torque between 33:67 and 50:50 front to rear, so 4H works on pavement. 4HLc and 4LLc lock the centre for loose surfaces. The modes are switched electrically.

Not from the factory on US trucks. BaT's 2001 Limited has a limited-slip rear, and 2003-on trucks have M-ASTC traction control. ARB lists a rear Air Locker for the 9.5-inch IRS diff in 2001–2006 Monteros, and one Expedition Portal owner runs ARB lockers with 4.90 gears.

faq.q: Should I buy a 3.5 or a 3.8?
faq.a: The 2001–02 3.5 is rated at 200 hp and 235 lb-ft, the 2003–06 3.8 at 215 hp and 248 lb-ft (BaT figures). The 3.8 trucks also get M-ASTC traction control, which owners rate highly. One owner says the 3.8 wants premium fuel and the 3.5 doesn't. Both are belt-driven and, owners say, interference engines.

faq.q: Is it the Montero that failed Consumer Reports' rollover test?
faq.a: Yes. In 2001 CR rated the Montero Limited 'Not Acceptable' after its test truck tipped up on two wheels in eight of nine runs at 36.7 mph or faster in a short-course avoidance manoeuvre. Mitsubishi disputed the method and quoted NHTSA's view that CR's test had no scientific basis, and Mitsubishi quoted a static stability factor equal to a three-star NHTSA rating.

faq.q: How often does the timing belt need changing?
faq.a: An owner quoting the manual says 105,000 miles for 2001–2006 Monteros, and owners say the engines are interference designs, so don't stretch it. Do the water pump, tensioner and seals at the same time. The 3.2 diesel uses a chain.

faq.q: What transmission fluid does it take?
faq.a: Owners insist on Mitsubishi Diaqueen SP-III and say other fluids cause slipping and torque-converter damage. Hyundai/Kia SP-III and Eneos SP are named as alternatives. AMSOIL lists 9.8 quarts total for the 2004 five-speed.

faq.q: What fuel economy should I expect?
faq.a: CarsGuide's expert puts normal consumption at 10 to 15 L/100 km. An NP 3.2 DI-D automatic owner reports about 10.5 L/100 km around town and 11 towing a caravan. Another owner says the petrol's range drops sharply when towing.

faq.q: Can I import a Japanese 3.2 diesel?
faq.a: Yes, once it's 25 years old by its own build date. As of October 2026 that covers trucks built up to about October 2001, and BaT has already sold a 1999 V68W 3.2 diesel in the US. Later trucks become eligible month by month. The EPA exemption is separate and needs the original configuration.

Not much yet. Twenty-four third-generation Monteros and Pajeros sold on Bring a Trailer between February 2022 and August 2026 brought $3,750 to $19,777, with a median of about $12,500. Low-mileage Limiteds sit at the top.

faq.q: Are there recalls I should check?
faq.a: In the US: the hydraulic brake booster accumulator on 2001–02 trucks (01V254001), a fuel-tank leveling valve that can leak on 2002–04 trucks (04V319000), and some label campaigns. Australia's REC-003136 covers the accumulator on 13,488 NM/NP Pajeros.
